title: SmartInsure - Model & Deployment Discovery
summary: Introductory discovery covering SmartInsure's use cases for claims automation and agent assist. Discussed open model choices (Llama variants, Mistral, RedPanda toy examples), context window needs (32k vs 128k), multilingual UX for English/Spanish/Portuguese, and tool-calling for policy lookups and PII-safe document retrieval. Security requirements (SOC2, SSO, KMS, data residency) drove interest in Redwood Dedicated vs Private. Agreed next steps: share pilot plan and cost estimate, run a 2-week benchmark using customer prompts, and provide security documentation.
transcript:
[00:00] Shawn (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Shawn from Redwood, with Maya and Ravi on the call. Quick roll call?
[00:07] Tom (SmartInsure): Hey Tom here, CTO at SmartInsure, Lina my ML engineer, Priya from security, Ethan product.
[00:13] Maya (SE): Awesome, appreciate the time. We put 45 minutes on the calendar to understand your model needs and deployment constraints.
[00:22] Lina: High level — we're building an agent-assist for claims adjusters and a doc ingestion pipeline to answer policy questions. Need 2 things: 1) long context for multi-doc claims (20k+ tokens) and 2) structured tool outputs for our downstream systems.
[00:36] Ravi: Got it. When you say "multi-doc claims", what's the typical chain? PDFs, medical forms, notes?
[00:42] Lina: PDFs (OCRed), emails, previous claim notes. Often chronological and we want the model to reference specific paragraphs. Sometimes Spanish docs.
[00:50] Ethan: Latency target is sub-1.2s for short lookups, but for full claim summarization 3-6s is okay. Cost sensitivity — we'd rather not overpay for every request.
[01:01] Shawn: Great, that maps well to features in Redwood: streaming for low-latency lookups, plus longer context variants for summarization. Quick question — are you open to open models or do you have a preference for provider models?
[01:11] Tom: Prefer open models where possible; legal wants control of data flow. But accuracy matters — for legal language and domain nuances, we need something validated.
[01:21] Priya: Security first: SOC 2 is table stakes, we need audit logs, SSO (SAML/OIDC), KMS integration and optional VPC for PII. Also data residency — some records must stay in us-east-1.
[01:35] Maya: Understood — Redwood Private keeps control on your VPC/on-prem and integrates KMS, our Dedicated offering gives reserved capacity in-region with strict tenancy. We can map those options to SLA/cost tradeoffs.
[01:45] Lina: On models — we tried a few internally: 13B Llama derivs were ok for long context but struggled with legalese; 70B Mistral-like models were better but expensive. Curious about quantized variants and whether Redwood supports tool-calling (i.e., function outputs we can parse reliably).
[02:03] Ravi: We support function/tool calling patterns. In hosted we offer structured output helpers and type enforcement; runtime will enforce return shapes where possible but you still should validate. In Dedicated/Private we can also run the same tool-calling shim but you'll want to run unit tests against the selected model variant.
[02:20] Tom: How about context windows — do we need 128k? what are practical tradeoffs?
[02:25] Maya: If you're frequently aggregating multiple full-length PDFs, 128k helps because you can keep raw doc context instead of heavy chunking. But it's heavier on memory and cost. For many workflows, smart KV caching + document embeddings with a 32k window for the active window is a good compromise: index older doc context into embeddings and selectively fetch relevant chunks.
[02:44] Lina: KV cache? we heard about prefix caching but not KV.
[02:48] Ravi: KV cache is our key-value cache for decoder past keys — it speeds up autoregressive decoding for repeated prefixes, helpful in assistant sessions where there's a lot of back-and-forth. Prefix caching is different (re-using prompt prefixes). Both lower token cost and latency.
[02:59] Priya: On compliance, if we do Private, do we still get Redwood Console for traces and rollouts? Auditing is critical.
[03:06] Maya: Yes, Private includes a control plane access pattern with audit logs forwarded to your logging endpoints. We can also push telemetry into your SIEM. There are options for log redaction and retention windows to meet legal needs.
[03:17] Ethan: Can you run multilingual models efficiently? We need English/Spanish/Portuguese and occasional Portuguese-BR. Latency and hallucinations in Spanish have been a pain in our PoCs.
[03:26] Ravi: A few paths: 1) pick a multilingual model (e.g., MPT-30B-multi style or later Llama mpts) 2) use language detection + language specific models for higher fidelity 3) augment with retrieval (RAG) and targeted prompt engineering. We can run language-specific evals in the pilot.
[03:44] Lina: For model selection, what open models do you recommend for our profile (70B vs 13B vs quantized 4-bit)?
[03:51] Maya: If you need top-domain accuracy and support multi-tool outputs, a 70B quantized variant (Q4_0 or Q4_K_M) often hits a sweet spot. 13B is cheaper for short lookups. We also recommend running a model-sweep during pilot: 13B quantized, 30B multilingual, and a 70B variant. We'll provide benchmark scripts.
[04:10] Tom: Cost — do you have unit economics per-call we can ballpark?
[04:15] Shawn: Quick rough math: for hosted, an avg short lookup maybe 50-200 tokens, a 13B quantized call could be few cents; a 70B summarization with 30k context could be several dollars if you hit full context often. Dedicated lowers per-token cost via reserved capacity. We'll send an estimated cost sheet with assumptions.
[04:32] Priya: Any concerns with PII escaping into logs? We want redaction pre-ingest and KMS so customer never sees plaintext in Redwood logs.
[04:40] Maya: For Private we can ensure PII never leaves your network. For Dedicated/Hosted we have redaction hooks and token-level redaction plus the ability to disable retention. We will also show how to configure token-level logs to avoid storing full user prompts.
[04:53] Ethan: Tool-calling — we need a deterministic output schema for a policy-lookup tool that returns {policy_id, clause_refs[], confidence}. Can Redwood guarantee structure?
[05:02] Ravi: We can enforce shape checks at the shim level. For full determinism you might want a verification step — e.g., the tool can return raw text plus extracted structure and then run a small deterministic validator. We also support function signatures for tool-calling that make parsing much simpler.
[05:18] Lina: Any limitations on the number of simultaneous tool calls? Our agents could call 3 different tools (policy DB, pricing calc, and doc fetch) in one turn.
[05:25] Maya: Concurrency depends on your concurrency tier and Dedicated pool sizing. For hosted we'll advise rate limit and batching settings. For Dedicated you can size the GPU pool for expected parallelism. Our console shows the per-token concurrency and queueing.
[05:38] Tom: What about low-latency lookups — you mentioned streaming. How deterministic is the early token output for assertions?
[05:45] Ravi: Streaming outputs still follow autoregressive generation; for exact-match assertions, best practice is to wait for finalization or run a short verification call. For small lookups we often do a 2-stage approach: quick streaming for UX and then an async verification for critical fields.
[06:00] Priya: Timeline — we're looking at a pilot within 6 weeks if security checks go quickly. Budget roughly mid-six-figures for a year if pilot succeeds.
[06:09] Shawn: Great — next steps we'll propose: pilot plan with model sweep, benchmark harness, cost estimate, security docs. We'll target a 2-week pilot and provide an SLO matrix.
[06:18] Ethan: Can you share an example pilot artifacts?
[06:21] Maya: Yes, we'll share a pilot playbook (link), benchmark scripts, and a sample dataset ingestion guide. We'll include a sample redaction pipeline and tool-call templates. Link: https://redwood.ai/pilot/smartinsure (placeholder).
[06:33] Lina: Good. For the benchmark, can you run our Spanish claim prompts?
[06:36] Ravi: Yes please send the prompt set and sample docs. We'll run the model sweep and include latency/cost/accuracy metrics per model.
[06:44] Tom: Any red flags from your side?
[06:47] Maya: Nothing major. The main risk is context vs cost tradeoff — if you insist on storing full claim history in every call, costs spike. Our recommendation: mix embeddings + caching, use 128k only when the UX requires it, and optimize tool-calls for deterministic outputs.
[07:05] Priya: We'll need SOC2 evidence and a network architecture diagram for Private. Also pen-test reports if available.
[07:13] Shawn: We'll attach SOC2, diagrams, and our standard pen-test summary.
[07:18] Ethan: Ok let's recap next steps...
[07:20] Tom: Recap: share pilot plan + pricing + security docs; SmartInsure to provide prompt set and sample documents; schedule a technical deep-dive with our infra team next week.
[07:30] Maya: Sounds good — we'll also include a recommended Dedicated sizing for expected concurrency and example rollback/rollout policy for canary.
[07:40] Lina: Thanks all, that was useful.
[07:42] Shawn: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the package later today.
[07:46] [call ends]
next_steps: Redwood to send pilot plan and cost estimate (Shawn)
SmartInsure to share Spanish prompt set and sample docs (Lina)
Schedule infra deep-dive with SmartInsure infra team for next week (Shawn + Tom)
Redwood to attach SOC2, pen-test summary, and network diagram (Shawn)
Run model sweep benchmarks on submitted prompts (Maya/Ravi)
